clue.text: Sometime pool worker's tipsy swimming time

indicators.note: something swimming moves about freely, so these letters drift out of their printed order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A tipsy pool attendant goes for a swim on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: The pool is not a swimming pool but a typing pool, the shared office of typists once found in large firms; 'sometime' marks the job as a thing of the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Offices once kept a typing pool, a room of staff producing letters on typewriters, and each member did that keyboard work.

clue.text: Band's experiment producing graphic material

parts.note: a tape is a band of material, plus the 's
a try is an attempt or experiment

explanation.surface: A band's experimental record gives rise to some graphic content.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' suggests a music group, but here it is a strip, as in tape; 'graphic material' suggests explicit content rather than woven pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: A woven wall hanging depicts scenes in thread, so it is fabric that carries pictures: cloth with images worked into it.

clue.text: Pieces spill over, first having been crammed in

indicators.note: something crammed in is stuffed inside another thing, so one piece sits within the other
turned over, as in a down clue read from the bottom up, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: to slop is to spill liquid
1st, written as I plus ST

explanation.surface: Pieces of something tumble over, with the first one squashed inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pieces' looks like fragments, but it is slang for handguns. 'First' becomes 1ST with the digit read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: In gangster slang a 'piece' is a handgun, so pieces are small firearms held in one hand.

clue.text: Perhaps Italian's lunch break's up, he and I keeping alcohol-free

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside the other
in a down clue going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a break is a gap, plus the 's
taken as written
TT, teetotal, means drinking no alcohol
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Italian worker's lunch break ends, and two people stay off the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunch break' reads as one phrase, but 'lunch' belongs to the definition and 'break' alone is the wordplay. TT, for teetotal, is the standard crossword shorthand for alcohol-free.
explanation.definitionFit: Long pasta is a typical Italian dish, so it is offered as one possible midday meal, with 'perhaps' flagging an example.

clue.text: One's fifty and retired on Friday?

parts.note: one is I, plus the 's
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
taken as written

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw or go back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: RE means on or about, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: Someone turns fifty and retires at the end of the working week.
explanation.walkthrough: Friday is not a day but Man Friday, the companion Robinson Crusoe meets on his island in Defoe's novel; the question mark flags that he is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Man Friday was a native of the island where Crusoe was shipwrecked, so he is one example of an island inhabitant.

clue.text: Good possibility of showing songs on the radio

indicators.note: radio is heard and not seen, so the words are judged by their sound

parts.note: showing is sporting, as in wearing; songs are chants, as at a football ground

explanation.surface: There is a decent chance some songs will be played on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showing' means wearing or displaying, as one sports a badge, and chants are the songs of a stadium crowd; spoken, the pair runs into the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A fair or reasonable likelihood of success is called this idiom, so it matches a decent prospect of something happening.

clue.text: Overlooking odd posts, valued X as sound

indicators.note: positions in a word are posts, and ignoring the odd ones leaves only the even ones

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
X is the Roman numeral for ten, and 10 written out looks like the letters I and O

explanation.surface: Someone skips some odd posts on social media and rates the sound highly.
explanation.walkthrough: X is worth ten; the digits 1 and 0 are read as the letters I and O, a visual trick rather than a standard abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is used for anything to do with sound recording or reproduction, so it stands for heard rather than seen content.

clue.text: Artist takes acid, tripping while quaffing wine

indicators.note: to quaff is to swallow a drink, so one piece goes down inside the other
someone tripping is stumbling or high on drugs, either way out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
vin is French for wine

explanation.surface: A painter drops acid and, high, gulps down wine as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acid' is the drug LSD in the surface, but it is only four letters to rearrange. 'Wine' is French here, the word on every bottle in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo, the Renaissance painter of the Mona Lisa, is known by this name from his home town, so he is a famous painter.

clue.text: Was frolicking Member ousted by Liberals turned over?

indicators.note: to be ousted by someone is to be thrown out and replaced by them, so one piece swaps in for another

parts.note: to romp is to play boisterously
MP, Member of Parliament
L is the abbreviation for Liberal, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A Member of Parliament who had been fooling about is thrown out by the Liberals.
explanation.walkthrough: The political surface hides the swap: MP leaves the middle of ROMPED and LL takes its place.
explanation.definitionFit: A vehicle or body that has rolled has flipped onto its side or back, so it has turned over completely.

clue.text: Author of "Three Points in Support of King Richard"

indicators.note: in a down clue a support sits underneath, so this part is placed below what follows it

parts.note: the name of three English kings
Dick is the usual short form of Richard
three compass points: east, north and south

explanation.surface: A writer is credited with a pamphlet titled as three arguments backing King Richard.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted title looks like a Ricardian tract; it is wordplay, with the compass points placed under the king and his short name.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the great Victorian novelist who wrote Oliver Twist and Great Expectations, so he is a celebrated writer.

clue.text: Taste shown by fancy sophisticate when rough set's not around

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or invented, so the remaining letters are made into something new
something not around is absent, so these letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
'rough' means the three letters of set may be scattered, not consecutive

explanation.surface: A refined person shows good taste when a rough crowd is absent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taste' looks like refinement, but it is a flavour. Strike S, E and T from SOPHISTICATE wherever they fall, then rearrange the nine letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: The green nut is a common ice-cream and dessert flavour, so it is one particular flavour you might choose.

clue.text: Rogue and daughter twisted on stage

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter

indicators.note: something twisted round faces the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a live performance is on stage

explanation.surface: A rascal and his daughter perform a contorted act on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' here simply joins the definition to the wordplay; D comes first, followed by LIVE turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A 'little devil' or 'you devil' is a mischievous scamp, so the word can mean a likeable rascal or scoundrel.

clue.text: Put out more even when short of nothing

indicators.note: to be short of something is to lack it, so that letter is removed

parts.note: more even means more level, flatter
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone puts out a more even result when falling just short of zero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' could mean annoyed, but here it is the verb for extinguishing a fire by cutting off its air.
explanation.definitionFit: You can douse flames by covering them with a blanket, starving the fire of oxygen, which extinguishes it.

clue.text: Best result of tight recount

indicators.note: tight is slang for drunk, and a drunken count jumbles things up

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: The best outcome of a close election is a recount.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' looks like an adjective and 'tight' like a close contest; Best is a verb, and tight means drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: To best an opponent is to beat them, and this verb means to defeat them heavily, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Once more, took police weapon back?

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: a Taser is a stun gun used by police

explanation.surface: An officer, once again, took back a confiscated police weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took' is used in the sense of taking an exam; once more makes it a repeat sitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Students who fail an exam can sit it again, and having done so they have taken that test a second time.

clue.text: In Cologne, one's seen both sides of St Albert?

indicators.note: something on both sides flanks the middle, so it wraps around the other piece

parts.note: ein is German for one, Cologne being a German city; the plural gives two copies
taken as written

explanation.surface: A visitor to Cologne sees both sides of a church dedicated to Saint Albert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'St Albert' reads as a saint's name, but St is wordplay and Albert alone is the definition. The plural 'ones' means two copies of EIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The physicist behind relativity was named Albert, so he is one famous bearer of that first name, as the question mark flags.

clue.text: Change schools, having lost child's focus with speech suppressed?

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so a letter is removed

parts.note: to school someone is to train them

indicators.note: a focus is the central point, so only the middle letter is kept

parts.note: the central letter of CHILD
mute means unable or not allowed to speak

explanation.surface: A child who has stopped talking moves to a new school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change schools' reads as moving school, but Change is the definition and 'schools' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To transmute is to transform one substance or form into another, as alchemists hoped to with lead, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Cold's piercing and doubled in France, with age and so on

indicators.note: something piercing goes through the middle, so it sits inside the other piece

parts.note: et is French for and, written twice
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
an era is an age

explanation.surface: Cold weather in France bites hard and seems twice as bad as the years go by.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes between the two copies of the French word, and ERA follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase, abbreviated etc., closes a list to show that further similar items are left unstated.

clue.text: Repeated romantic "I do" — I reprised cuddles reflexively

indicators.note: a reflex action bends back on itself, so the letters run backwards
to cuddle is to hold close, so the words hold the letters within them

parts.note: the last letter of romantic through to the first three of reprised

explanation.surface: A couple renew their vows with a second loving 'I do', hugging each other.
explanation.walkthrough: The wedding picture of renewed vows suits 'Repeated', which is in fact the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something periodic happens at intervals, again and again, so it recurs regularly in the way a repeated thing does.

clue.text: Barking tends not entirely to come under E6, that's clear

indicators.note: not the whole thing means a part is missing, so the last letter goes
in a down clue coming under means sitting below, so this part follows the other

parts.note: E plus VI, the Roman numeral for six

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go haywire

parts.note: the word without its final letter

explanation.surface: Barking, in east London, tends to fall partly under the E6 postcode, plainly.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a district of east London and E6 a London postcode, so the clue reads as local geography; Barking is the anagram signal and the 6 is a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evident is plain to see and obvious, which is what clear means when describing a fact or truth.

clue.text: Refit west-facing home that's broken in

indicators.note: breaking in means forcing a way inside, so one piece enters the other

parts.note: at means in, as in at home

indicators.note: across clues read west to east, so facing west means reading right to left

parts.note: a pad is slang for someone's home

explanation.surface: A burgled west-facing house needs a refit.
explanation.walkthrough: The final 'in' does double service: it is part of 'broken in' and also the word that becomes AT, which surrounds the turned-round home.
explanation.definitionFit: To refit something is to modify or re-equip it for a new purpose, so it is a synonym of altering to suit.

clue.text: Union that might shortly represent you and me

definitions.text: Union that might shortly represent you and me

parts.words: Union that might shortly represent you and me
parts.note: surface reading: a trade union that will soon speak for us workers
setter's reading: the federal union whose short form, the two-letter abbreviation, is the pronoun for you and me

explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' suggests a trade union and 'shortly' soon; in fact 'shortly' means abbreviated, and the US abbreviation spells the pronoun us.
explanation.definitionFit: The United States is a federal union of fifty states, and its everyday name is the continent it occupies.

clue.text: Advanced maths in revision causing complaint

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for advanced, as in A level

indicators.note: a revision reworks a text, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Revising advanced maths leaves a student complaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' suggests grumbling, but it is the medical sense of an ailment. 'Maths' is the British word for math.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is an illness, and this chronic lung condition that causes wheezing is one.

clue.text: Singing mass maybe, Jagger creating upheaval

indicators.note: singing is voiced out loud, so the words are judged by their sound

parts.note: mass is size, Mick Jagger is the Rolling Stones singer

explanation.surface: Mick Jagger singing a Mass would cause quite a stir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' suggests a church service, but it is bulk, a kind of size; 'maybe' flags it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Seismic describes earthquakes and, by extension, any change so great that it shakes things up dramatically.

clue.text: One might find even letters written in emails dear?

definitions.text: One might find even letters written in emails dear?

indicators.note: even letters are those in second, fourth and later even positions

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Someone complains that even sending an email costs too much.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a tight-fisted person grudges even the cost of messages, and the even letters spell that person.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarder who hates spending money would think even free electronic messages expensive, which the whole sentence describes.

clue.text: Paying visit to chateau, stereotypically bleak

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside a place, so the letters are found within the words

parts.note: the end of chateau and the start of stereotypically

explanation.surface: A visit to a French castle is, as you might expect, rather grim.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the comma, from the last two of chateau into the start of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere describes something plain, stark and without comfort, which is what bleak means of a place or outlook.

clue.text: Mini, say, won't accommodate wide parts of body

indicators.note: refusing to accommodate means not letting something in, so that letter is left out

parts.note: wheels is slang for a car, and the Mini is a classic British small car
W is the cricket abbreviation for a wide

explanation.surface: A small car won't fit people with broad bodies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wide parts of body' reads as one phrase, but 'wide' belongs to the wordplay. A wide is a cricket delivery out of the batter's reach, scored W.
explanation.definitionFit: The rounded back parts of the feet are anatomical features, so they are some of the bits that make up a person.

clue.text: Unique monastic scripture substituted by former partner

indicators.note: something substituted is swapped out, so one piece is replaced by another

parts.note: monks live a secluded life
RE, religious education, the school subject
an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: A one-off religious text is replaced by something from an ex.
explanation.walkthrough: Scripture is RE, the British school subject Religious Education, often called Scripture in older schools.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exclusive is not shared or available elsewhere, so it is one of a kind, which is what unique means.

clue.text: Star agitated at skiers or skaters I managed

indicators.note: agitated means shaken up, so these letters are jumbled
managed means handled or arranged, so these letters are reorganised too

parts.note: first set of fodder, taken as written
second, alternative set of fodder with the same eight letters

explanation.surface: A famous person gets rattled by skiers or the skaters someone manages.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate anagrams give the same answer, joined by 'or'; either alone would do.
explanation.definitionFit: The typographical symbol shaped like a little star is named from the Greek for small star, so the two match.

clue.text: State of retro TV station once seen in article

indicators.note: retro means harking back, so the letters run backwards
something seen in a place is inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
Dave is a UK television channel, renamed U&Dave in 2024

explanation.surface: An article reports on the condition of an old-fashioned television station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like condition; it is a US state. 'Retro' applies to everything after the container is built, not just the channel name.
explanation.definitionFit: The desert territory containing Las Vegas is one of the fifty members of the United States federation.
